HTTP Verbs and Status Codes as a Contract

The verb-to-action convention, and why a status code carries meaning, not just success/failure.

If the URL names a resource (previous slide), the HTTP method names the action. A handful of verbs cover practically every case:

Verb On /tickets (the collection) On /tickets/:id (one resource)
GET list all tickets fetch one ticket
POST create a new ticket —
PUT/PATCH — update a ticket
DELETE — delete a ticket

This project builds GET and POST on /tickets first (this lesson's actual deliverable); PUT/PATCH/DELETE and the equivalents for other resources (comments, tags, ...) arrive with full CRUD in Week 3.

The other half of the contract is the status code — not just "200 = worked, anything else = broken," but a specific vocabulary a client can act on programmatically:

  • 200 OK — a GET succeeded.
  • 201 Created — a POST succeeded and made a new resource.
  • 400 Bad Request — the request itself was invalid (e.g. a required field missing) — the client's fault.
  • 404 Not Found — no resource exists at that URL.
  • 500 Internal Server Error — something broke on the server's side.

A Laravel web route can get away with being loose about this, because a human looking at a rendered page can tell success from failure either way. A JSON API can't rely on that — the status code (paired with a JSON error body) is how a client program tells what happened, since there's no page to read. Every one of these codes already appears somewhere in this project's code — 404 in notFound.js, 400 and 201 in the ticket controller, 500 as the errorHandler's default — and the next topic is where you'll meet them for real.
